details:
MANGLO — Nature Seen from Space

The Challenge: Seeing Beyond the Clouds

How can we protect ecosystems if we cannot consistently observe how they change?

In El Salvador, mangroves and wetlands support biodiversity, protect coastal environments, and sustain local communities. However, optical satellite monitoring faces a significant limitation: cloud cover.

Our analysis of Cerrón Grande revealed that 45.5% of 77 rainy-season optical images had less than half the reservoir visible. We also identified a 15-day period, from July 7 to July 22, 2026, without a sufficiently clear optical observation.

This raised a fundamental question: what if we could continue monitoring these ecosystems even when clouds block our view?

Our Solution: MANGLO

MANGLO is an interactive environmental monitoring platform built around Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations from the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission.

Unlike optical sensors, SAR can acquire observations during the day or night and through cloud cover.

We developed MANGLO to explore three environmentally significant regions of El Salvador: Barra de Santiago, Bahía de Jiquilisco, and Cerrón Grande.

The platform combines satellite observations, temporal comparisons, interactive maps, environmental indicators, artificial intelligence, and 3D visualizations in a single experience.

Our goal is to make complex geospatial information accessible while preserving the scientific context and limitations needed for responsible interpretation.

Beyond Visualization: Artificial Intelligence

MANGLO goes beyond displaying satellite imagery. We developed machine learning tools to interpret patterns in radar observations.

For mangrove mapping, we developed MangroveNet, a U-Net deep learning model that uses multi-date NISAR HH/HV radar observations. We trained it on Bahía de Jiquilisco and Cerrón Grande and tested it on Barra de Santiago, a site the model never encountered during training.

There, MangroveNet achieved an F1 score of 0.82 for the mangrove class against ESA WorldCover reference labels. It estimated 23.1 km² of mangrove coverage, compared with 24.4 km² in the reference map.

This evaluation explores the model's ability to generalize to a geographically distinct area rather than simply reproducing patterns from its training locations.

For Cerrón Grande, we developed an experimental Random Forest model to identify vegetation on water using NISAR observations and optical reference data from Sentinel-2.

The model achieved a mean F1 score of 0.544, compared with 0.440 for a fixed-rule baseline, representing a relative improvement of 23.6%. It outperformed the baseline on all seven evaluated dates.

We also incorporated an experimental radar-to-photo AI model that transforms radar observations into approximate optical-style images to support visual exploration. These generated images are interpretations, not actual optical observations.

A Real-World Example

On September 15, 2026, the evaluated optical image of Cerrón Grande was completely obscured by clouds. However, our NISAR processing workflow generated an experimental estimate of approximately 14.66 km² of vegetation on water.

This example illustrates how radar observations can provide useful information when optical imagery is unavailable. However, the estimate still requires field validation and does not constitute confirmed identification of a particular plant species.

To turn these observations into meaningful environmental insights, we combined satellite missions, scientific datasets, artificial intelligence, and interactive visualization tools. Each technology plays a specific role in making MANGLO both scientifically grounded and accessible.

Technology and Development

MANGLO integrates multiple Earth observation datasets and scientific tools:

  • NASA-ISRO NISAR: L-band HH/HV radar observations for monitoring under cloudy conditions.
  • Sentinel-2: complementary optical satellite observations.
  • ESA WorldCover: land-cover reference information.
  • Global Mangrove Watch: historical mangrove extent information spanning 1996–2020, incorporating JAXA L-band radar observations.
  • NASA ORNL DAAC: mangrove biomass and canopy-height datasets used to support exploratory blue-carbon estimates.
  • NASA SWOT: reservoir water-level observations.
  • NASA ECOSTRESS: land-surface temperature observations.
  • NASA POWER: rainfall information.
  • MangroveNet (U-Net): deep learning for experimental mangrove classification.
  • Random Forest: machine learning for experimental vegetation detection.
  • Radar-to-photo AI: approximate optical-style image generation from radar observations.

We used Python with PyTorch, scikit-learn, Rasterio, and earthaccess for scientific data processing and machine learning. The interactive web platform was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, incorporating Leaflet, Chart.js, Three.js, globe.gl, and satellite.js. Its main features include interactive environmental maps, temporal comparisons, scientific indicators, 3D terrain views, and a 3D globe visualizing NISAR's orbital trajectory.

MANGLO also provides a guided tutorial, a general exploration view, and a scientific mode, with interfaces available in English and Spanish.

Creativity, Scientific Responsibility, and Impact

MANGLO's innovation lies in connecting radar observations, artificial intelligence, historical environmental data, and interactive scientific visualization within a unified platform.

Instead of requiring users to consult multiple specialized sources independently, MANGLO enables them to explore processed environmental information from three Salvadoran territories in one place.

The platform also connects current observations with historical mangrove records, complementary satellite measurements, and experimental indicators related to vegetation and blue carbon.

Scientific transparency was a central consideration throughout development. Changes in radar backscatter do not automatically indicate environmental degradation, experimental classifications are not substitutes for field measurements, and generated optical-style images should not be mistaken for real satellite photographs.

Our results are evaluated against reference datasets, and their interpretation must account for the limitations of those references.

MANGLO is intended to support researchers, students, environmental institutions, and local communities seeking to understand changes in their territories.

By making Earth observation data more accessible, we aim to encourage environmental research, education, and informed conservation efforts.

Our Vision

The Earth doesn't wait for clouds to clear before it changes. Neither should the way we observe it.

As Jane Goodall said:

"Only if we understand, can we care. Only if we care, will we help."

MANGLO: Observe to understand. Understand to protect.
